questions.stem: Consider the following statements about INFLATION INDICES in India. 1. CPI-Combined is compiled and released by the National Statistical Office under MoSPI. 2. CPI-IW (Industrial Workers) is released by the Labour Bureau and anchors Dearness Allowance. 3. WPI current series has base year 2011-12. 4. The RBI's flexible inflation target of 4 % ±2 is anchored on CPI-Combined. Which statements are correct?

options.option_text: 1, 2 and 4 only
1 and 4 only
2 and 3 only

questions.explanation: All four are correct. CPI-Combined — NSO/MoSPI. CPI-IW — Labour Bureau (base 2016 = 100). WPI current base 2011-12 (revised from 2004-05; proposal under discussion to shift to 2017-18 or 2022-23). The RBI's Monetary Policy Framework Agreement 2015 and subsequent statutory framework under RBI Act (Section 45ZA) set a CPI-Combined target of 4 % with a ±2 % tolerance band.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: ASSERTION (A): When the RBI raises the REPO RATE, banks typically raise their lending rates, cooling aggregate demand. REASON (R): A higher repo rate makes it costlier for banks to borrow overnight from the RBI, so they pass the higher cost through to customers.

options.option_text: Both A and R are true, R is the correct explanation
Both A and R are true, R is NOT the correct explanation
A is true, R is false
Both are false

questions.explanation: Repo rate = rate at which RBI lends to banks against government securities (very short-term, mainly overnight). When the repo rises, banks' marginal cost of funds rises, and under the MCLR (and now EBLR for retail loans) regime, lending rates tend to follow. Higher borrowing cost → less credit-fuelled demand → cooling effect on inflation.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which of the following is most characteristic of STAGFLATION?

options.option_text: High growth + low inflation
Low growth + low unemployment + low inflation
Low / stagnant growth + high unemployment + high inflation
High growth + high unemployment + deflation

questions.explanation: Stagflation = stagnation + inflation. Its hallmark is simultaneous high unemployment (or low growth) AND high inflation — something the original Phillips curve couldn't explain. Classic case: 1970s OECD after oil shocks. Supply-side shocks (like a spike in crude) are a common trigger.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Consider the following statements about the MONETARY POLICY COMMITTEE (MPC). 1. It has six members: three from the RBI and three external members appointed by the Central Government. 2. The MPC meets at least four times in a financial year. 3. Decisions are taken by majority, with the RBI Governor having a casting vote in case of a tie. 4. The MPC was constituted under the RBI Act, 1934 as amended in 2016. Which are correct?

options.option_text: 1, 2 and 4 only
1, 3 and 4 only
2 and 4 only

questions.explanation: All four correct. Composition: Governor (Chair) + Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy + one RBI officer + three external members (academics/experts, 4-year terms, non-renewable). MPC meets at least 4 times a year (in practice every 2 months). Casting vote with Governor on tie. Amendment to RBI Act in 2016 (Finance Act 2016) inserted Chapter IIIF (Sections 45Z–45ZO).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a quantitative tool of monetary policy in India?

options.option_text: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)
Moral Suasion
Open Market Operations (OMO)

questions.explanation: Moral suasion is a QUALITATIVE (selective) tool — the RBI persuades banks to act in certain ways without formal mandate. Quantitative tools are the levers that directly affect the overall volume of credit: CRR, SLR, repo/reverse repo, OMO, MSF, Bank Rate. Other qualitative tools: margin requirements, credit rationing, direct action.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: If the CPI-Combined was 150 in March 2025 and 156 in March 2026 (base 2012 = 100), the year-on-year CPI inflation in March 2026 is closest to:
questions.explanation: YoY inflation = (new − old)/old × 100 = (156 − 150)/150 × 100 = 6/150 × 100 = 4.0 %. The trap is using (156 − 150)/100 = 6 % (wrong base). Always divide by the EARLIER index, not the index-base of 100.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Using the Fisher relation (real rate ≈ nominal − inflation), in which case does the NOMINAL rate UNDERSTATE the real return?

options.option_text: Inflation is negative (deflation)
Inflation is zero
Inflation is positive
Inflation equals the nominal rate exactly

questions.explanation: Real = nominal − π. If π < 0 (deflation), real > nominal → nominal UNDERSTATES the real return. If π > 0 (typical inflation), real < nominal → nominal OVERSTATES the real return. If π = 0, real = nominal exactly.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which component is EXCLUDED from 'core inflation' but retained in 'headline inflation' as measured in India?

options.option_text: Housing rent and the imputed rent sub-index in CPI
Food and beverages, and fuel and light categories of CPI
Clothing, bedding and footwear sub-group within CPI
Miscellaneous services such as education and healthcare

questions.explanation: Core inflation strips out the volatile food and fuel/energy categories from headline CPI to reveal the underlying, persistent inflation trend. Housing (Option A) and clothing (Option C) remain in the core basket; they are not excluded. Miscellaneous services (Option D) are also part of core. Only food and fuel are removed, as they are subject to seasonal and global supply shocks that distort the structural price signal.

questions.stem: Under India's flexible inflation targeting framework, formalised via the RBI (Amendment) Act 2016, what is the mandated TARGET and TOLERANCE BAND assigned to the Monetary Policy Committee?

options.option_text: 3% CPI inflation target with a tolerance band of ±1%
4% CPI inflation target with a tolerance band of ±2%
5% WPI inflation target with a tolerance band of ±2%
4% WPI inflation target with a tolerance band of ±1%

questions.explanation: The 2016 amendment to the RBI Act mandated a 4% CPI-Combined inflation target with a ±2% tolerance band, giving an operative range of 2%–6%. The benchmark is CPI, not WPI — WPI plays no role in India's formal inflation targeting regime. Option A uses the right index but wrong numbers. Options C and D both incorrectly substitute WPI as the target variable.

questions.stem: Consider the following statements comparing WPI and CPI-Combined in India. 1. WPI does not cover services, while CPI-Combined includes services such as health and education. 2. The base year for WPI is 2011-12 and for CPI-Combined is 2012. 3. WPI assigns a higher weight to food articles than CPI-Combined does. Which of the above statements is/are CORRECT?

options.option_text: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Statement 3 is incorrect
Statements 2 and 3 are correct; Statement 1 is incorrect
Statement 1 alone is correct; Statements 2 and 3 are false
Statements 1, 2 and 3 are each factually correct

questions.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: WPI tracks only traded goods; CPI-Combined includes services (health, education, transport). Statement 2 is correct: WPI base year is 2011-12 and CPI-Combined base year is 2012. Statement 3 is incorrect: CPI-Combined assigns about 46% weight to food and beverages, whereas WPI's aggregate food weight is roughly 24% — so WPI gives significantly lower weight to food. Option B is a strong distractor because it correctly pairs Statement 2 while smuggling in the wrong Statement 3.

questions.stem: A sharp rise in global crude oil prices pushes up transportation and manufacturing costs, causing the general price level to rise. Which type of inflation does this represent, and why is conventional monetary tightening a LIMITED remedy for it?

options.option_text: Demand-pull; tightening cuts money supply but cannot lower global oil prices
Cost-push; tightening curbs demand but cannot eliminate the underlying supply-side cost
Structural inflation; tightening raises bond yields but bypasses the root cause
Built-in inflation; a wage-price spiral requires income policy rather than rate hikes

questions.explanation: Rising crude oil prices are a supply shock — the textbook example of cost-push inflation. Monetary tightening raises borrowing costs and suppresses aggregate demand, offering partial relief, but cannot reduce the fundamental input cost (crude prices). Aggressive tightening risks recession without solving the supply-side problem. Option A misidentifies the type as demand-pull. Option D (built-in/wage-price spiral) is a structurally different mechanism where inflation is self-perpetuating through wage negotiations, not triggered by an external commodity shock.

questions.stem: When the RBI conducts an Open Market Operation (OMO) by PURCHASING government securities from commercial banks, what is the PRIMARY macroeconomic effect?

options.option_text: Bank reserves shrink, credit creation contracts, and inflation is reined in
Liquidity is injected into the banking system, money supply expands, and yields decline
Government's fiscal deficit is directly monetised through the RBI's purchase
Bank lending rates automatically rise following the securities purchase by RBI

questions.explanation: When RBI buys G-secs in the secondary market, it credits the selling banks' accounts with newly created money — bank reserves rise, broad money supply expands, bond prices increase, and yields fall. This is an expansionary (liquidity-injecting) OMO. Option A describes contractionary OMO (RBI selling securities). Option C is a frequent misconception: OMO operates in the secondary market on already-issued securities, so it does not directly finance the government's deficit — that would be deficit monetisation through primary issuance.

questions.stem: Which among the following MOST ACCURATELY describes the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) interest-rate corridor as operative in India after the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) was introduced in April 2022?

options.option_text: Reverse repo rate is the operative floor, repo rate the anchor, MSF the ceiling
SDF rate is the operative floor, repo rate the policy anchor, MSF rate the ceiling
MSF rate forms the floor, and the SDF rate forms the ceiling of the corridor
Repo rate serves as both floor and ceiling, with SDF and MSF sitting outside the band

questions.explanation: Since April 2022, the SDF (Standing Deposit Facility) replaced the reverse repo as the operative floor of the LAF corridor; the SDF rate is set at repo minus 25 basis points. The repo rate remains the policy anchor (midpoint). The MSF (Marginal Standing Facility) at repo plus 25 bps continues as the ceiling. Banks park surplus funds with RBI at the SDF rate and borrow emergency overnight funds at the MSF rate. Option A describes the pre-April 2022 structure; the reverse repo rate still exists but the SDF is now the active floor.

questions.stem: In monetary economics, the 'sacrifice ratio' is used to evaluate the real cost of anti-inflationary policy. Which of the following CORRECTLY defines it?

options.option_text: The tax revenue foregone when the government provides fiscal stimulus to boost growth
The cumulative GDP loss required to reduce the inflation rate by one percentage point
The fall in foreign exchange reserves when RBI intervenes to defend the rupee's value
The share of a repo rate hike that is actually transmitted to bank lending rates

questions.explanation: The sacrifice ratio measures the real economic cost of disinflation: how many percentage points of output (GDP) — or equivalently, unemployment — must be lost to achieve a one-percentage-point reduction in inflation. A high sacrifice ratio means tighter monetary policy is very costly in growth and employment terms. Option D is a common distractor: it describes the monetary policy transmission ratio — a related but entirely distinct concept. Option C describes FX intervention impact on reserves, which has no connection to the sacrifice ratio.
